content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Reuse reduces duplicated logic but the abstraction should match the unit of work: full workflow, composite action, custom action, or ordinary script. Reuse the right abstraction: reusable workflows compose jobs; composite actions bundle steps; JavaScript or container actions package executable behavior. Define inputs, outputs, permissions, and versions explicitly. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Comparing reusable workflows, composite actions, and scripts
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

content_blocks.code:
# .github/workflows/reusable-checks.yml
name: Reusable checks
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      runtime:
        required: false
        type: string
        default: "3.12"
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Run common checks for ${{ inputs.runtime }}"
content_blocks.expected_output: A caller can invoke this workflow and supply the optional `runtime` input; replace the placeholder with reusable checks.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a test repository or static validation first. Confirm the snippet matches the repository, runner, permissions, and current GitHub documentation.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove temporary test workflows and never carry test credentials or sample outputs into production.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to why reuse workflow logic?. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain why reuse workflow logic?, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Package shared workflow logic behind clear input/output contracts and maintained versions.

content.task: Apply why reuse workflow logic? to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Reuse reduces duplicated logic but the abstraction should match the unit of work: full workflow, composite action, custom action, or ordinary script.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Reuse reduces duplicated logic but the abstraction should match the unit of work: full workflow, composite action, custom action, or ordinary script. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Reuse reduces duplicated logic but the abstraction should match the unit of work: full workflow, composite action, custom action, or ordinary script.

Reuse the right abstraction: reusable workflows compose jobs; composite actions bundle steps; JavaScript or container actions package executable behavior. Define inputs, outputs, permissions, and versions explicitly.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
